notes.front: What is Compute Engine?
notes.back: Google Cloud's infrastructure as a service product, offering self-managed virtual machine instances and bare metal instances.
notes.explanation: It supplies the machines themselves, with Linux or Windows operating systems and durable storage, for you to configure and run.
notes.example: Like renting an empty office floor in a well-run building: the building is maintained for you, but you furnish and run the floor yourself.
notes.source: Compute Engine overview, “Compute Engine overview”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine is an infrastructure as a service (IaaS) product that offers self-managed virtual machine (VM) instances and bare metal instances. Compute Engine offers VMs with a KVM hypervisor, operating systems for both Linux and Windows, and durable storage options.

notes.front: In Compute Engine, what are machine types?
notes.back: The predefined configurations you choose from when you create a compute instance, grouped into machine series within machine families.
notes.explanation: The overview arranges them as a hierarchy: a family contains series, and each series contains its predefined machine types.
notes.example: Like choosing a car: first the range, then the model line, then the exact trim with its engine and seats already fixed.
notes.source: Compute Engine overview, “Compute Engine machine types”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine provides a comprehensive set of machine families, each containing machine types to choose from when you create a compute instance. Each machine family is comprised of machine series and predefined machine types within each series.

notes.front: What is Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s managed implementation of Kubernetes, the open source platform for orchestrating containers.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes itself came from Google, which drew on years of running production workloads on its in-house cluster manager, Borg.
notes.example: Like hiring a managing agent for a block of flats: you still decide who lives where, but someone else keeps the lifts and boilers running.
notes.source: GKE overview, “GKE overview”
notes.evidence: GKE is a managed implementation of the Kubernetes open source container orchestration platform. Kubernetes was developed by Google, drawing on years of experience operating production workloads at scale on Borg

notes.front: What was GKE Enterprise, and what has happened to it?
notes.back: A former GKE offering. Its features are now part of standard GKE or are add-on products, and GKE no longer has editions.
notes.explanation: So there is no separate enterprise tier to buy today: the capabilities sit inside GKE itself or alongside it.
notes.example: Like a premium software bundle that was retired once its features were folded into the standard product.
notes.source: GKE Enterprise release notes, “GKE Enterprise release notes”
notes.evidence: The features that were part of GKE Enterprise have become part of the standard Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) offering, or are products or features that you can use in addition to GKE. GKE is a single offering, without different editions or tiers.

notes.front: What is Cloud Run?
notes.back: A fully managed application platform for running your code, function or container on Google's scalable infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Any programming language works, provided the code can be built into a container image.
notes.example: Like a taxi rank for your code: you bring the passenger (the container) and cars appear when needed, with no fleet of your own to maintain.
notes.source: What is Cloud Run, “What is Cloud Run”
notes.evidence: Cloud Run is a fully managed application platform for running your code, function, or container on top of Google's highly scalable infrastructure. You can deploy code written in any programming language on Cloud Run if you can build a container image from it.

notes.front: What is Cloud Run functions?
notes.back: The latest version of Google Cloud's functions product, in which each function is deployed as a service on Cloud Run.
notes.explanation: The name reflects that functions now run on Cloud Run itself, as Cloud Run services.
notes.example: Like a motion-sensor light: it does one small job when something happens, but it runs on the same wiring as the rest of the house.
notes.source: Compare Cloud Run functions, “Comparison”
notes.evidence: Cloud Run functions, is the latest version of functions, deployed as a service on Cloud Run.

notes.front: What does the study guide describe App Engine as?
notes.back: A Google Cloud service for building and deploying web apps.
notes.explanation: Its focus is the web app itself; the study guide sets it beside Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions as ways to host application code.
notes.example: Like a ready-built shop unit for a web app: you move your goods in, but the building is already standing.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is AlloyDB Omni?
notes.back: A downloadable database software package that runs a streamlined version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL in computing environments you manage.
notes.explanation: It shares its core components with the fully managed AlloyDB service on Google Cloud, but you run it in your own chosen environment.
notes.example: Like buying a restaurant chain's recipe kit to cook in your own kitchen, instead of eating at the restaurant.
notes.source: AlloyDB Omni overview, “AlloyDB Omni overview”
notes.evidence: AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable database software package that lets you deploy a streamlined version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL in computing environments that you manage. AlloyDB Omni and the fully managed AlloyDB service on Google Cloud share the same core components.

notes.front: What is BigQuery Omni?
notes.back: A way to run BigQuery analytics on data stored in Amazon Simple Storage Service or Azure Blob Storage.
notes.explanation: It reaches that data in the other public cloud through BigLake tables.
notes.example: Like an auditor who travels to a branch office to read its files, instead of having every box shipped to head office.
notes.source: Introduction to BigQuery Omni, “Introduction to BigQuery Omni”
notes.evidence: With BigQuery Omni, you can run BigQuery analytics on data stored in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Azure Blob Storage using BigLake tables.

notes.front: According to the study guide, what upfront investment does Compute Engine need, and what does each of its virtual machines act as?
notes.back: None; each virtual machine works as a complete operating system.
notes.explanation: This is the business value the study guide gives it: you get whole machines to run on Google infrastructure without buying hardware first.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Compute Engine's cost benefit: you pay only for {{c1::the resources that you use}}, and there are no up-front costs.
notes.back: the resources that you use
notes.explanation: The overview adds that it offers a variety of pricing options to fit your budget.
notes.source: Compute Engine overview, “Compute Engine overview”
notes.evidence: Cost-effectiveness: Compute Engine offers a variety of pricing options to fit your budget. Also, you only pay for the resources that you use, and there are no up-front costs.

notes.front: What are two of Compute Engine's machine families?
notes.back: Any two, for example general-purpose and memory-optimised.
notes.explanation: The overview lists six: general-purpose, compute-optimised, network-optimised, storage-optimised, memory-optimised and accelerator-optimised.
notes.source: Compute Engine overview, “Compute Engine machine types”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine offers general-purpose, compute-optimized, network-optimized, storage-optimized, memory-optimized, and accelerator-optimized machine families.

notes.front: In GKE, what are a cluster's nodes?
notes.back: Compute Engine virtual machines, grouped together to form the cluster.
notes.explanation: Applications are packaged into containers, which run on those nodes.
notes.source: GKE overview, “How GKE works”
notes.evidence: A GKE environment consists of nodes, which are Compute Engine virtual machines (VMs), that are grouped together to form a cluster. You package your apps (also called workloads) into containers.

notes.front: In GKE, what does Google Cloud manage for you, and what does Autopilot mode add?
notes.back: The control plane and system components; in Autopilot mode, your worker nodes as well.
notes.explanation: The documentation calls Autopilot the recommended way to run GKE, and in it node management also passes to Google.
notes.source: GKE overview, “How GKE works”
notes.evidence: In GKE, Google Cloud manages the control plane and system components for you. In Autopilot mode, which is the recommended way to run GKE, Google Cloud also manages your worker nodes.

notes.front: Must you build a container image yourself to deploy code to Cloud Run?
notes.back: No. For supported languages, the source-based deployment option builds the container for you.
notes.explanation: The documentation calls building images optional, and says the built container follows the best practices for your language.
notes.source: What is Cloud Run, “What is Cloud Run”
notes.evidence: In fact, building container images is optional. If you're using Go, Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, Ruby, or a supported framework you can use the source-based deployment option that builds the container for you, using the best practices for the language you're using.

notes.front: What are two example uses the documentation gives for Cloud Run services?
notes.back: Any two, for example websites and web applications, and microservices.
notes.explanation: The documentation says services suit code that handles requests, events or functions, which covers both.
notes.source: What is Cloud Run, “When to use Cloud Run services”
notes.evidence: Cloud Run services are great for code that handles requests, events, or functions. Example use cases include: Websites and web applications Build your web app using your favorite stack, access your SQL database, and render dynamic HTML pages. APIs and microservices

notes.front: If a Cloud Run service receives no incoming requests, {{c1::even the last remaining instance is removed}}; this is called scale to zero.
notes.back: even the last remaining instance is removed
notes.explanation: The trade-off: when a request next arrives, Cloud Run must create a new instance, which can slow those first responses.
notes.source: What is Cloud Run, “Scale to zero”
notes.evidence: If there are no incoming requests to your service, even the last remaining instance will be removed. This behavior is commonly referred to as scale to zero. When a new request arrives for a service with no active instances, Cloud Run creates a new instance. This process can increase the response time for these initial requests

notes.front: How finely does Cloud Run charge for the processor and memory allocated to an instance, and what does an unused service cost?
notes.back: In 100-millisecond steps; with no minimum instances configured, an unused service costs nothing.
notes.explanation: This is why the documentation calls scale to zero attractive for economic reasons.
notes.source: What is Cloud Run, “Pay-per-use pricing for services”
notes.evidence: Scale to zero is attractive for economic reasons since you're charged for the CPU and memory allocated to an instance with a granularity of 100ms. If you don't configure minimum instances, you're not charged if your service is not used.

notes.front: Cloud Run functions was formerly named {{c1::Cloud Functions (2nd gen)}}.
notes.back: Cloud Functions (2nd gen)
notes.explanation: The comparison table gives each version’s former product name; the 1st gen was Cloud Functions (1st gen).
notes.source: Compare Cloud Run functions, “Concepts”
notes.evidence: Former product name Cloud Functions (2nd gen) Cloud Functions (1st gen)

notes.front: What is Cloud Run functions (1st gen)?
notes.back: The original version of functions, formerly Cloud Functions (1st gen), with limited event triggers, runtimes and configurability.
notes.explanation: Those limits on triggers, runtimes and configuration are what set it apart from the current version.
notes.source: Compare Cloud Run functions, “Comparison”
notes.evidence: Cloud Run functions (1st gen), formerly known as Cloud Functions (1st gen), is the original version of functions with limited event triggers, runtimes, and configurability.

notes.front: When you deploy a function directly onto Cloud Run, what happens to it?
notes.back: It is automatically built as a container and deployed as a Cloud Run service.
notes.explanation: You supply the function; the container build and the deployment as a service are done for you.
notes.source: Compare Cloud Run functions, “Comparison”
notes.evidence: By deploying functions directly onto Cloud Run, your functions are automatically built as containers and deployed as a Cloud Run service.

notes.front: Which benefit of modern cloud app development, in the study guide's list, splits one large block of code into small, independent services?
notes.back: Microservices architecture.
notes.explanation: Microservices are small, autonomous services that talk over a network, in place of one monolithic codebase.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of modern cloud app development, in the study guide's list, speeds up releases by leaving upkeep to the cloud provider?
notes.back: Deployment with managed services.
notes.explanation: With managed services the provider looks after maintenance and operations, and the team concentrates on the app.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of modern cloud app development, in the study guide's list, lets an app take on more users by growing its capacity with demand?
notes.back: Scalability.
notes.explanation: The exam guide describes this benefit as enhanced scalability, paired with resilience.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of modern cloud app development, in the study guide's list, gives teams a view of a running app's health and the means to run it?
notes.back: Monitoring and management tools.
notes.explanation: It is the operations item on the study guide's list, beside architecture, deployment, pricing, scalability and availability.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two environments where AlloyDB Omni can run?
notes.back: Any two, for example your private data centres and any public cloud.
notes.explanation: The documentation credits its portability; the list also includes laptops and cloud-based virtual machine instances.
notes.source: AlloyDB Omni overview, “AlloyDB Omni overview”
notes.evidence: AlloyDB Omni's portability lets you run it in many environments, including the following: - Your private data centers - Any public cloud - Your laptop - Cloud-based VM instances

notes.front: Who manages AlloyDB Omni, and how can you move to the fully managed service later?
notes.back: You do: it is self-managed. You can migrate to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL with any PostgreSQL-supported migration method.
notes.explanation: Choosing Omni therefore leaves the fully managed database version open as a later upgrade.
notes.source: AlloyDB Omni overview, “AlloyDB Omni use cases”
notes.evidence: AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and is self-managed. To upgrade to the fully managed database version, you can choose to migrate your AlloyDB Omni database to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL using any PostgreSQL-supported migration methods

notes.front: Why does BigQuery Omni save on outbound data transfer costs?
notes.back: Because the data doesn't move: it is not copied across clouds, and queries run in the region where it resides.
notes.explanation: The same fact speeds up insights, since nothing has to be copied across clouds first.
notes.source: Introduction to BigQuery Omni, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Performance. You can get insights faster, because data is not copied across clouds, and queries run in the same region where your data resides. Cost. You save on outbound data transfer costs because the data doesn't move.

notes.front: Who deploys and manages the clusters that run BigQuery Omni?
notes.back: Google does: BigQuery Omni is serverless, so you provision no resources and manage no clusters.
notes.explanation: It works the same way as the rest of BigQuery in this respect.
notes.source: Introduction to BigQuery Omni, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Serverless architecture. Like the rest of BigQuery, BigQuery Omni is a serverless offering. Google deploys and manages the clusters that run BigQuery Omni. You don't need to provision any resources or manage any clusters.

notes.front: Besides AlloyDB Omni, which database product does the study guide list as supported in hybrid and multicloud environments?
notes.back: Cloud SQL.
notes.explanation: The study guide's full list is AlloyDB Omni, BigQuery Omni, GKE Enterprise, Cloud SQL and Looker.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which business intelligence platform does the study guide list among Google Cloud products supported in hybrid and multicloud environments?
notes.back: Looker.
notes.explanation: It is the one analytics-presentation tool on a list otherwise made up of databases, BigQuery Omni and GKE Enterprise.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A news website's traffic jumps tenfold for a few hours whenever a big story breaks. It wants virtual machines it can add for the rush and remove afterwards, without running its own hardware. Which product fits?
notes.back: B) Compute Engine
notes.choices:
A) BigQuery Omni
B) Compute Engine
C) Looker
D) AlloyDB Omni
notes.choicesExplained: A) BigQuery Omni runs BigQuery analytics on data in other clouds; it does not supply virtual machines. C) Looker is a business intelligence platform. D) AlloyDB Omni is a database package, not a source of virtual machines.
notes.explanation: The overview names exactly this: scale the number of instances up for a sudden rise in traffic and remove them when they are no longer needed.
notes.source: Compute Engine overview, “Compute Engine overview”
notes.evidence: Scalability: Scale the number of compute resources as needed without having to manage your own infrastructure. This is useful for businesses that experience sudden increases in traffic, because you can quickly add more instances to handle the increase and remove the instances after they are no longer needed.

notes.front: An engineering team finds that no predefined general-purpose machine type gives the balance of processor and memory its simulation needs. What does Compute Engine offer?
notes.back: A) A custom machine type with its own processor and memory settings, available for some machine series
notes.choices:
A) A custom machine type with its own processor and memory settings, available for some machine series
B) Use a Spot VM of the nearest predefined type
C) Rewrite the simulation as Cloud Run functions
D) Nothing: only predefined types can be used
notes.choicesExplained: C) Cloud Run functions host small, single-purpose code, not a long simulation that needs a particular machine shape. B) A Spot VM is discounted capacity that can be reclaimed; it changes price and availability, not the balance of processor and memory. D) Custom machine types do exist, for some machine series.
notes.explanation: The overview offers custom machine types for exactly the case where a preconfigured general-purpose type does not meet your needs.
notes.source: Compute Engine overview, “Compute Engine machine types”
notes.evidence: If a preconfigured, general-purpose machine type doesn't meet your needs, then you can create a custom machine type with customized CPU and memory resources for some of the machine series.

notes.front: A platform team runs dozens of containerised services. It wants managed Kubernetes but still needs to configure the networking, scaling, hardware and security of the infrastructure beneath them. Which product fits best?
notes.back: A) Google Kubernetes Engine
notes.choices:
A) Google Kubernetes Engine
B) Cloud Run functions
C) App Engine
D) BigQuery Omni
notes.choicesExplained: C) App Engine is a service for building and deploying web apps, not a Kubernetes platform. B) Cloud Run functions host small, single-purpose functions triggered by events. D) BigQuery Omni runs analytics on data in other clouds.
notes.explanation: GKE is described as ideal when you need to configure the infrastructure under containerised apps, while Google manages components such as the control plane.
notes.source: GKE overview, “When to use GKE”
notes.evidence: GKE is ideal if you need a platform that lets you configure the infrastructure that runs your containerized apps, such as networking, scaling, hardware, and security. GKE provides the operational power of Kubernetes while managing many of the underlying components, such as the control plane and nodes, for you.

notes.front: A consultant tells a bank it must buy a separate 'GKE Enterprise edition' to get GKE's fleet features. What does current Google Cloud documentation say?
notes.back: D) GKE is a single offering with no editions; the former Enterprise features are part of standard GKE or add-on products
notes.choices:
A) The consultant is right: GKE Enterprise is a separate paid edition
B) The Enterprise features were withdrawn and are no longer available
C) GKE Enterprise has been renamed Cloud Run
D) GKE is a single offering with no editions; the former Enterprise features are part of standard GKE or add-on products
notes.choicesExplained: A) The documentation says GKE has no editions or tiers, so there is nothing separate to buy. C) Cloud Run is a separate serverless platform, not a renamed GKE edition. B) The features were folded into GKE or offered alongside it, not withdrawn.
notes.explanation: The GKE Enterprise release-notes page says exactly this.
notes.source: GKE Enterprise release notes, “GKE Enterprise release notes”
notes.evidence: The features that were part of GKE Enterprise have become part of the standard Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) offering, or are products or features that you can use in addition to GKE. GKE is a single offering, without different editions or tiers.

notes.front: A personnel team's leave-request app is used for a few minutes a day. It runs on Cloud Run, and the team wants no charges during the idle hours. Which setting achieves this?
notes.back: A) Leave minimum instances unset, so the service scales to zero when idle
notes.choices:
A) Leave minimum instances unset, so the service scales to zero when idle
B) Move it to Compute Engine virtual machines that run all day
C) Switch the service to instance-based billing
D) Set minimum instances so the app is always warm
notes.choicesExplained: D) Minimum instances keep instances running, so the service never scales to zero. B) Virtual machines left running all day are charged all day. C) Instance-based billing charges for each instance's whole lifetime, so it does not cut idle charges.
notes.explanation: Billing is for the processor and memory allocated to instances, and with no minimum instances configured an unused service is not charged.
notes.source: What is Cloud Run, “Pay-per-use pricing for services”
notes.evidence: Scale to zero is attractive for economic reasons since you're charged for the CPU and memory allocated to an instance with a granularity of 100ms. If you don't configure minimum instances, you're not charged if your service is not used.

notes.front: Each time a photo is uploaded to a storage bucket, an online shop wants a few lines of code to make a thumbnail: one small job per event. Which product matches the study guide’s description?
notes.back: B) Cloud Run functions
notes.choices:
A) Compute Engine
B) Cloud Run functions
C) GKE
D) Looker
notes.choicesExplained: A) Compute Engine gives you whole virtual machines to run and manage, far more than one small event handler needs. C) GKE is a managed Kubernetes platform for containerised apps. D) Looker is a business intelligence platform.
notes.explanation: The study guide describes Cloud Run functions as hosting simple, single-purpose functions attached to events one at a time, which is this job exactly.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A start-up wants its hosting bill to rise and fall with actual use instead of paying for servers in advance. Which benefit of modern cloud app development, in the study guide’s list, is it after?
notes.back: A) Pay-as-you-go pricing
notes.choices:
A) Pay-as-you-go pricing
B) Monitoring and management tools
C) Microservices architecture
D) Highly available and resilient
notes.choicesExplained: B) Monitoring and management tools are about seeing and running the app, not how it is billed. C) Microservices architecture is about how the code is structured. D) High availability and resilience are about staying up when parts fail.
notes.explanation: Paying for what is actually used, rather than buying capacity ahead, is what pay-as-you-go pricing means.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An online bank's app must keep serving customers when one of its components fails. Which benefit of modern cloud app development, in the study guide’s list, is this?
notes.back: B) Highly available and resilient
notes.choices:
A) Scalability
B) Highly available and resilient
C) Deployment with managed services
D) Pay-as-you-go pricing
notes.choicesExplained: A) Scalability is about growing capacity with demand, not surviving a failure. C) Deployment with managed services is about releasing faster by leaving upkeep to the provider. D) Pay-as-you-go pricing is about how the app is billed.
notes.explanation: Staying up through a component failure is resilience; the exam guide pairs it with scalability.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A hospital group must keep its patient database on its own premises for regulatory reasons, but wants a high-performance PostgreSQL it could later move to a Google Cloud managed service. Which product fits?
notes.back: B) AlloyDB Omni
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Run
B) AlloyDB Omni
C) Looker
D) BigQuery Omni
notes.choicesExplained: A) Cloud Run is a managed platform for running code on Google's infrastructure, not a database for the hospital's premises. D) BigQuery Omni runs BigQuery analytics on data in other public clouds. C) Looker is a business intelligence platform, not a database.
notes.explanation: Running a scalable, high-performance PostgreSQL on-premises because of regulatory or data sovereignty requirements is the first use case the documentation lists.
notes.source: AlloyDB Omni overview, “AlloyDB Omni use cases”
notes.evidence: You need a scalable, high-performance version of PostgreSQL that you must run on-premises due to regulatory or data sovereignty requirements.

notes.front: A retailer keeps its sales logs in Amazon's object storage, and its analysts already use BigQuery. It wants to query the logs with BigQuery without copying the raw data out of that cloud. Which product fits?
notes.back: A) BigQuery Omni
notes.choices:
A) BigQuery Omni
B) AlloyDB Omni
C) Cloud Run
D) Compute Engine
notes.choicesExplained: B) AlloyDB Omni is a PostgreSQL database package, not a way to query data in another cloud with BigQuery. C) Cloud Run runs code and containers; it is not an analytics engine. D) Compute Engine supplies virtual machines, on which the analysts would have to build their own query system.
notes.explanation: With BigQuery Omni the data stays in your own Amazon or Azure account, and you need not move or copy it out of that public cloud.
notes.source: Introduction to BigQuery Omni, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Security and data governance. You manage the data in your own AWS or Azure subscription. You don't need to move or copy the raw data out of your public cloud.

notes.front: How does paying for GKE differ between Autopilot mode and Standard mode?
notes.back: Autopilot: you pay only for the compute your running Pods request. Standard: you pay for all resources on the nodes.
notes.explanation: In Standard mode the charge follows the nodes, regardless of what the Pods request.
notes.source: GKE overview, “Benefits of GKE”
notes.evidence: In Autopilot mode, pay only for the compute resources your running Pods request. In GKE Standard mode, you pay for all resources on nodes, regardless of Pod requests.

notes.front: Which GKE mode of operation does Google recommend, and when should you use the other one?
notes.back: Autopilot. Use Standard only if you have a specific need to manage the node pools and clusters manually.
notes.explanation: In Autopilot, Google Cloud manages your nodes and provides a workload-focused, cost-optimised, production-ready experience.
notes.source: GKE overview, “Modes of operation”
notes.evidence: Use the fully managed Autopilot mode, in which Google Cloud manages your nodes for you and provides a workload-focused, cost-optimized, production-ready experience. Only use Standard mode if you know you have a specific need to manually manage the node pools and clusters.

notes.front: How does a Cloud Run service differ from a Cloud Run job?
notes.back: A service answers requests at a stable endpoint and scales automatically; a job runs tasks, manually or on a schedule, to completion.
notes.explanation: A service keeps responding for as long as requests arrive, while a job does its work and stops.
notes.source: What is Cloud Run, “Services, jobs, worker pools, and instances”
notes.evidence: Responds to HTTP requests sent to a unique and stable endpoint, using stateless container instances that support both dynamic autoscaling and manual scaling, also responds to events and functions. Job Executes parallelizable tasks that are executed manually, or on a schedule, and run to completion.

notes.front: How do Cloud Run's request-based and instance-based billing settings differ?
notes.back: Request-based: no charge while an instance isn't processing requests, plus a per-request fee. Instance-based: the instance's whole lifetime is charged, with no per-request fee.
notes.explanation: Both are billing settings that you can enable on a Cloud Run service.
notes.source: What is Cloud Run, “Pay-per-use pricing for services”
notes.evidence: Request-based If an instance is not processing requests, you're not charged. You pay a per-request fee. Instance-based You're charged for the entire lifetime of an instance. There's no per-request fee.

notes.front: How does the study guide distinguish Cloud Run from Cloud Run functions?
notes.back: Cloud Run runs containerised apps that handle many events at once; Cloud Run functions hosts simple, single-purpose functions handling events one at a time.
notes.explanation: That is the study guide's framing; Google's comparison page is more exact: current Cloud Run functions take up to 1,000 concurrent requests per instance, and only 1st gen handles one at a time.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
